If you want a complicated argument, note that "you cannot lose weight if you are hungry" is logically equivalent to "you cannot be hungry if you are losing weight". What evolutionary reason would there be for this? Hunger is an extraordinarily basic instinct because non-human animals rely only on instinctual drives, not reason, to survive. If an animal doesn't experience hunger, it will waste away and die without understanding why. Under your sister's theory that hunger goes away if you stop eating, a predator that doesn't catch food for a few days would stop wanting food and thus die. This doesn't sound conducive to survival. Perhaps hunger fades a bit, but it surely can't go away until you're on death's door. Any mutation that lead to hunger going away as soon as you're losing weight (when glycogen is depleted, I assume), would surely be lethally maladaptive to wild animals. Ask her to explain why hunger going away once you're losing weight wouldn't defeat the entire evolutionary point of hunger.

(The hunger mechanism isn't perfect, and humans are a clever lot, so it is possible to lose weight with little or no hunger by carefully calculated actions like getting lots of fiber and water and a low-carb diet, or by unnaturally concentrated chemicals like caffeine, nicotine, amphetamines, and other stimulants. In fact, I'm pretty sure that all four combinations are possible: (1) lose weight with hunger, (2) gain/maintain weight without hunger, (3) lose weight without hunger, and (4) gain/maintain weight with hunger. Your sister is arguing that (1) is impossible. It's important to remember that she is the one making the extraordinary claim. You are not making the claim that the hunger mechanism is perfect and only (1) and (2) are possible. You're merely claiming that the hunger mechanism is not perfectly backward, not that it's perfect.)
